title: "Translating ITSM and Risk Metrics for Executives"

## Two meetings, one Tuesday

Your calendar for Tuesday has two blocks that used to make you nervous in different ways. At
10:00, your CIO (chief information officer) wants fifteen minutes on "where things stand" with
the eQMS (electronic quality-management system) before he signs off on this quarter's risk
register. At 2:00, you're presenting the same system's status to the exec quality council —
Quality leadership, the Medical Director, Compliance — as part of their own standing review.

Same system. Same week. Two audiences who have never sat in the same room for this conversation
and, this quarter, don't need to — except that the thing you tell them has to be the *same thing*,
or you have a problem far worse than either meeting going badly.

Here's what you're actually walking into both rooms with: one open item. The eQMS's quarterly
access-review control — the check that catches a stale account or a mismatched permission before
it sits unnoticed — is built, documented, and sitting on the record as `grc-frameworks-and-
risk-management` left it: implemented, not yet exercised on its first scheduled cycle, accepted by
you as a named, time-bound residual risk with a 30-day remediation window. Nothing about that fact
has changed since the day you authorized it. What changes, room to room, is what each audience
needs to *do* with it.

Your Quality Analyst (QA) catches you reviewing both decks the night before. "These don't read
anything alike," she says, flipping between them. You brace for a problem — until she finishes the
sentence. "Good. They shouldn't. They just can't disagree."

That's the whole job of this module: tell the same fact twice, correctly, to two rooms that care
about different things — without ever letting "different things" slide into "different stories."

## Why this matters — and the ITSM bridge

Name the failure this module exists to prevent, because it's not the one people usually picture.
The failure isn't telling the CIO bad news. It's telling the CIO and the quality council
*inconsistent* news — the same underlying fact, described with a different owner, a different
date, or a different severity, because each deck got written to sound good to its particular
audience instead of translated from one shared set of facts. The moment anyone — an auditor, an
assistant who sits in both meetings, your own QA cross-checking two decks the night before —
compares the two tellings and finds them sitting even slightly apart, every number in both decks
becomes suspect. Not just this one. All of them, going forward. That's not a bad meeting. That's a
credibility problem that outlives the meeting by years.

You already own two ITSM (IT service management) concepts that, read together, are exactly this
discipline. `coaching-and-reporting-upward` already taught you to spot a **"watermelon" report** —
green on the summary tile, red the moment you open the ticket underneath — and to separate
**system measures from personal performance measures**, because the instant a system number
becomes someone's personal target, people stop reporting it honestly. This module is the same
instinct, aimed sideways instead of upward: not *which* numbers you report, but *how the same
number sounds* in two rooms that measure success differently. Think of it as **audience
segmentation**, a concept you already run constantly in IT communications — the same outage gets a
two-line banner for end users, a detailed timeline for the service desk, and a full post-incident
review for the CAB (change advisory board). Nobody calls that spin. It's spin only the moment the
*facts* differ between audiences, not just the framing.

One more piece of vocabulary worth being precise about, because this module will lean on it hard:
a **nonconformance**, in AABB's (Association for the Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies) Quality
System Essentials (QSE) vocabulary, is a finding that something didn't meet a defined requirement —
graded by severity, tracked to closure. This item isn't quite that, and getting the distinction
right matters for both rooms: nothing has gone wrong yet. The access review hasn't failed; it
simply hasn't run its first cycle. That's a genuine difference from a CAPA (corrective and
preventive action), which `poams-and-capas` already drew precisely — and it's a difference you'll
need to hold onto in both meetings, not soften in one and sharpen in the other.

## The rule in plain English

One fact. Two translations. Zero daylight between them on anything that actually matters: what the
finding is, who owns it, what the date is, and what happens if the date passes.

Translating for an audience means choosing what to **emphasize** and what to **leave in the
appendix** — a CIO doesn't need AABB's vocabulary explained to him line by line; a quality council
doesn't need a primer on NIST's (National Institute of Standards and Technology) RMF (Risk
Management Framework) task numbering. Translating never means choosing what to **change**. The
finding, the owner, the date, and the current status are not translatable content — they're the
fixed point both versions orbit. Everything else — which details lead, which get a sentence versus
a paragraph, which framework's vocabulary carries the explanation — is where the actual
translation work happens.

## A note on citations: none new, one fact reused exactly

This module introduces no new regulatory source, standard, or framework — the same discipline this
entire course has held since module 1. It draws on exactly one piece of already-locked content:
`poams-and-capas`'s own finished POA&M (plan of action and milestones) entry for the eQMS, built in
`grc-frameworks-and-risk-management` from NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2's Task A-6 and never altered since.
Nothing below reopens that entry, adds a field to it, or restates it differently than the source
module built it. Read `poams-and-capas` for the verbatim NIST text and the full reasoning behind
every field; this module only translates the finished table, field for field.

## The one fact, read verbatim from the record

Before either translation, here's the actual source both of them have to match — quoted exactly as
`poams-and-capas` built it, not paraphrased, not re-decided:

| Field | Locked entry |
|---|---|
| **Finding / deficiency** | The quarterly eQMS access-review control (account and identity management) is implemented and documented, but has not yet been exercised on its first scheduled cycle. |
| **Planned action** | Run the first quarterly access review against the eQMS's current account list, across all three sites, and report the results. |
| **Resources required** | The systems administrator's own time; the review mechanism already exists from Implement — no new tool, budget, or staffing. |
| **Recommendation for completion** | After authorization — the Director authorized the eQMS for production now, with this action scheduled to follow, not a precondition to go-live. |
| **Owner** | The systems administrator. |
| **Milestone / scheduled completion date** | Within 30 days of the Director's authorization decision. |
| **Reviewed and accepted by** | The Director, as Lakeshore's own authorizing official. |
| **Status / closure rule** | A clean result closes the acceptance. A finding becomes a new, immediate finding on its own record. If the 30-day date passes with no review run, the authorization itself is reopened. |

Every word in both briefings below has to trace back to one of these eight rows. If a sentence in
either deck can't point to a row in this table, it doesn't belong in the deck — it's invented, and
invented content is exactly what turns a translation into two different stories.

## Translation one: briefing the CIO

Your CIO is smart, cares about risk and cost, and doesn't know AABB or FDA (Food and Drug
Administration) specifics — he needs the fact converted into business risk, operational exposure,
a dated commitment, and a trigger that tells him when this becomes his problem before it already
is one.

Here's what you actually say, in the room, in under a minute:

> "One open item on the eQMS risk register this quarter. The quarterly access review that's
> supposed to catch a stale account or a mismatched permission across our three sites is built and
> ready, but it hasn't run its first cycle yet. I accepted that as a time-bound risk, not an open
> one — the systems administrator runs the review within 30 days of go-live, using the tool we
> already built, so there's no new budget ask and no new timeline risk to anything else we're
> running. If it comes back clean, this item closes. If it finds something — one stale account,
> one wrong permission — that becomes its own tracked item on its own timeline, not something we
> pretend we already caught. The only thing that puts this back on your desk unscheduled: if the
> 30 days pass and the review hasn't run. That reopens my own authorization decision for the whole
> system, and you'd hear about it the same day."

Notice what this version leads with and what it skips. It leads with **operational exposure in
plain terms** (a stale account sitting undetected on a system that holds CAPA records and audit
logs across three sites), **the dollar and schedule impact** (none — no new spend, no new
timeline), **the date**, and **the specific trigger that would escalate to him**. It skips AABB's
vocabulary entirely and never says the word "nonconformance" — not because the finding is being
softened, but because that word doesn't help a CIO act on this; "reopens the authorization" does.

A risk-register line reads the same way, compressed to the format he actually reviews:

| Risk register field | Entry |
|---|---|
| **Item** | Unreviewed access control, eQMS, all three sites |
| **Status** | Accepted, time-bound (not open/unmitigated) |
| **Owner** | Systems administrator |
| **Target date** | 30 days from authorization |
| **Cost/schedule impact** | None — existing mechanism, no new resourcing |
| **Escalation trigger** | Date missed → system authorization reopened → Director notifies CIO same day |
| **Decision needed from CIO today** | None — informational only, unless the trigger fires |

## Translation two: briefing the exec quality council

The same room, the same week, needs the same fact dressed in a completely different vocabulary —
and needs to hear, explicitly, that it isn't a CAPA, because this council will reach for that word
the instant you say "gap."

> "One item to flag on the eQMS, tracked as a time-bound control gap against account and identity
> management, not a nonconformance and not a CAPA — nothing has deviated; the access-review control
> simply hasn't completed its first scheduled cycle yet. It's tracked the same way NIST's own
> framework tracks an item like this: a POA&M, sitting right next to our CAPA log in rigor,
> though it isn't identical in structure — it doesn't carry CAPA's own required root-cause analysis
> or formal effectiveness check, because nothing has happened yet that would need either one. Owner
> is the systems administrator. Closure date is 30 days from my own authorization sign-off, which is
> already on record. If the review comes back clean, the item closes on that record. If it finds
> something — a stale account, a wrong permission — that becomes a new, separately tracked finding,
> not folded quietly into this one. If an AABB assessor or FDA investigator ever asks about the
> eQMS's own control state between now and then, this entry is the answer: a self-identified,
> actively tracked item, not something we'd be catching cold."

This version leads with **AABB/FDA framing** (is this a nonconformance? no — and here's precisely
why not), **the audit-trail implication** (this is the artifact that answers an assessor's
question, the same point `building-an-inspection-ready-service-catalog-and-cmdb` already proved
about a self-identified gap grading better than one found cold), and **the same owner and date**,
stated with equal weight, not buried. It skips cost and schedule impact almost entirely — the
council doesn't evaluate this item on budget; it evaluates whether Lakeshore's own control
discipline would survive a reviewer's question.

## Side by side: same facts, different emphasis

| | CIO needs to hear | Quality council needs to hear |
|---|---|---|
| **The finding itself** | Unreviewed access control, 3 sites — identical wording either way | Identical wording — a control gap, not yet a nonconformance |
| **Owner** | Systems administrator | Systems administrator — same name, same sentence |
| **Closure date** | 30 days from authorization | 30 days from authorization — same date, same number |
| **What closes it** | A clean review result | A clean review result — identical closure rule |
| **What a miss produces** | A new tracked item, its own timeline | A new finding, tracked on its own record |
| **Escalation trigger** | Missed date reopens the authorization → reaches the CIO that day | Missed date reopens the authorization → would be the exact thing an assessor asks about if found unreported |
| **Primary framing** | Business/operational risk, cost, schedule | AABB/FDA vocabulary, audit-trail defensibility |
| **What's emphasized** | No new budget, no new timeline risk | Not a CAPA, not a nonconformance — a self-identified, time-bound item |
| **What's de-emphasized (but never hidden)** | NIST vocabulary, POA&M-versus-CAPA structure | Dollar cost, schedule impact |

Read the middle three rows again, because they're the whole point: **owner, date, and closure
rule never move.** Everything above and below those rows is a legitimate difference in what each
audience needs emphasized. Those three rows are not a place to exercise judgment about framing —
they're the fixed facts that make both tellings the same story.

## What an assessor or your CIO would actually look for

Here's the check that actually catches a bad translation, and it's simpler than it sounds: **put
both decks next to each other and read only the owner, the date, and the closure rule.** An AABB
assessor pulling your management-review minutes alongside your IT risk register would do exactly
this — not because she suspects dishonesty, but because cross-checking two records that describe
the same system is a completely ordinary part of how a thorough assessment works. If the systems
administrator's name, the 30-day date, or the closure criterion differ by even a detail between
the two documents, that mismatch itself becomes the finding — not the underlying access-review gap,
which was always a defensible, well-managed item, but the fact that Lakeshore's own records about
it don't agree. A bad answer, in that moment, sounds like "oh, that's just how we phrased it for
that audience." A reviewer hears that sentence as evidence that framing and facts aren't being kept
separate anywhere else in your records either.

Your CIO would make the identical check, for a different reason: if he ever compares notes with
the Medical Director or Compliance and hears a different severity, a different date, or a different
owner than the one you gave him, the damage isn't to this one risk item. It's to every number you
bring him afterward.

## Common traps

**"Translating for the audience means softening it for whichever room is less technical."** No —
and this is the trap this entire module exists to name. Softening changes the *severity*; framing
changes the *vocabulary*. The CIO version above doesn't downplay the finding — it states plainly
that a miss reopens the system's own authorization. The quality-council version doesn't inflate it
into a nonconformance it isn't. Both versions carry the identical weight of the identical fact.
If you ever catch yourself making one version sound more serious or less serious than the other to
manage a room's reaction, you've stopped translating and started spinning — and the two decks will
eventually meet each other.

**"Since the CIO doesn't know AABB vocabulary, I can simplify by changing the date or the owner to
make the explanation cleaner."** Also no. Simplify the *explanation* — skip RMF's task numbering,
skip CAPA's effectiveness-check structure where it isn't needed. Never simplify the *facts*. A
date, an owner, and a closure rule are not complicated enough to need rounding off, and rounding
them off is exactly the kind of small inconsistency a careful reviewer catches first.

## What this means for your job

- **Before any briefing leaves your hands, write the fixed row first — finding, owner, date, status
  — and check every other sentence in the deck against it.** If a sentence can't trace back to that
  row, it's invented, not translated.
- **Lead each version with what that audience needs to act on, not with a watered-down version of
  the whole record.** A CIO acts on cost, schedule, and escalation triggers. A quality council acts
  on AABB/FDA framing and audit-trail defensibility. Neither needs the other's lead paragraph, but
  both need the same facts underneath it.
- **Say explicitly, in the quality-council version, what this is not** — not a CAPA, not yet a
  nonconformance — the same precision `poams-and-capas` built the distinction with. A vague "this
  is sort of like a deviation" invites exactly the kind of confusion a sharp council member will
  catch and ask about.
- **Before you walk into either room, imagine the other room's deck sitting open next to it.** If
  anything you're about to say would read as a different story next to the other version, fix it
  before the meeting, not after someone notices.
- **Treat a self-identified, consistently-described item as the asset it actually is.** The same
  finding, told the same way twice, is evidence of a functioning control environment. Told two
  different ways, it becomes evidence of the opposite — regardless of how well-managed the
  underlying item actually is.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your QA asks whether the exec-quality-council briefing should call this item a "nonconformance" to make sure Quality leadership takes it seriously. Should it?

No — and this is worth being precise about, not just cautious. Nothing has deviated: the access-
review control is implemented and documented; it simply hasn't completed its first scheduled cycle
yet. Calling it a nonconformance would overstate the fact to make the room react more strongly,
which is exactly the kind of "translation" that's actually spin. The honest version — a time-bound
control gap, tracked with the same rigor a nonconformance would require (named owner, closure date,
defined closure rule) but not itself one — takes the finding seriously without inventing a severity
that isn't there.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Does NIST, AABB, or FDA require Lakeshore to brief this item to the CIO and the exec quality council in two separately worded versions?

No. Nothing in NIST's RMF, AABB's QSE framework, or FDA regulation specifies how Lakeshore
communicates an accepted residual risk to its own internal audiences, or requires two versions at
all — Lakeshore could, in principle, read the exact same POA&M table aloud in both rooms. Building
two translated versions is Lakeshore's own choice, made because each audience acts faster and more
confidently on a version that speaks its own vocabulary — not because any regulator or standard
demands a dual-audience briefing format.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: A colleague suggests that since the CIO's version never uses the word "nonconformance," it must be describing a less serious issue than the quality council's version. Is that colleague right?

No. The word choice reflects vocabulary, not severity. Both versions describe the identical
finding, owned by the identical person, closing on the identical date, under the identical closure
rule. The CIO's version is phrased in cost/schedule/escalation terms because that's what he acts
on; the quality council's version is phrased in AABB/FDA terms because that's what it acts on. If
the actual severity differed between the two tellings — a faster date in one, a softer owner in the
other — that would be the real problem this module is built to catch, not a matter of which words
got used.
:::
